rows.subtopic: Nature of Roots and the Discriminant
rows.stem: The value of k for which the equation \(kx^2 - 6x - 4 = 0\) has real and equal roots, is
rows.solution:
Real and equal roots need the discriminant to be zero: \((-6)^2 - 4 \times k \times (-4) = 0\), that is \(36 + 16k = 0\).

So \(k = -\dfrac{36}{16} = -\dfrac{9}{4}\), which is option (C) \(-\dfrac{9}{4}\).

rows.subtopic: Section Formula and Ratio of Division
rows.stem: The line segment joining the points \(P(-4, -2)\) and \(Q(10, 4)\) is divided by y-axis in the ratio
rows.solution:
Every point on the y-axis has x-coordinate 0. Let the y-axis divide PQ in the ratio \(k : 1\). Then

\(\dfrac{10k + (-4)}{k + 1} = 0\), so \(10k = 4\) and \(k = \dfrac{2}{5}\).

The ratio is \(2 : 5\), which is option (A) \(2 : 5\).

rows.subtopic: Forming a Quadratic Polynomial from its Zeroes
rows.stem: If the zeroes of a polynomial \(p(x)\) are \(-3\) and 8, then \(p(x)\) equals
rows.solution:
A polynomial with zeroes \(-3\) and 8 is a non-zero multiple of \((x + 3)(x - 8)\).

\((x + 3)(-x + 8) = -(x + 3)(x - 8)\), which is zero at \(x = -3\) and \(x = 8\). (The choice \(a(x^2 + 5x - 24) = a(x + 8)(x - 3)\) has zeroes \(-8\) and 3.)

This is option (B) \((x + 3)(-x + 8)\).

rows.subtopic: Tangent to a Circle
rows.stem: In the given figure, PQ is tangent to the circle with centre O. S is a point on the circle such that \(\angle SQT = 55^\circ\). The m \(\angle QPS\) is
rows.figureNote: REQUIRED - that PS passes through the centre O, and that T lies on PQ produced beyond Q, is shown only in the drawing. Page idx 4.
rows.solution:
The radius OQ is perpendicular to the tangent PT, so \(\angle OQS = 90^\circ - 55^\circ = 35^\circ\). Since \(OQ = OS\) (radii), \(\angle OSQ = \angle OQS = 35^\circ\).

P, Q and T lie on one line, so \(\angle PQS = 180^\circ - 55^\circ = 125^\circ\).

In triangle PQS, \(\angle QPS = 180^\circ - 125^\circ - 35^\circ = 20^\circ\), which is option (B) \(20^\circ\).

rows.subtopic: Criteria for Similarity of Triangles
rows.stem: Devansh proved that \(\Delta ABC \sim \Delta PQR\) using SAS similarity criteria. If he found \(\angle C = \angle R\), then which of the following was proved true ?
rows.solution:
SAS similarity uses an equal angle and the sides that include it in proportion. The equal angles are \(\angle C\) and \(\angle R\); the sides including \(\angle C\) are AC and BC, and those including \(\angle R\) are PR and QR.

So \(\dfrac{AC}{PR} = \dfrac{BC}{QR}\), that is \(\dfrac{AC}{BC} = \dfrac{PR}{QR}\), which is option (D) \(\dfrac{AC}{BC} = \dfrac{PR}{QR}\).

rows.subtopic: Mean of Grouped Data
rows.stem: While calculating mean of a grouped frequency distribution, step deviation method was used \(\left(\dfrac{x - a}{h} = u\right)\). It was found that \(\bar{x} = 64\), \(h = 5\) and \(a = 62.5\). The value of \(\bar{u}\) is
rows.solution:
In the step-deviation method \(\bar{x} = a + h\bar{u}\).

\(64 = 62.5 + 5\bar{u}\), so \(\bar{u} = \dfrac{1.5}{5} = 0.3\), which is option (C) \(0.3\).

rows.subtopic: Surface Area of a Combination of Solids
rows.stem: A conical cavity of maximum volume is carved out from a wooden solid hemisphere of radius 10 cm. Curved surface area of the cavity carved out is (use \(\pi = 3.14\))
rows.figureNote: ILLUSTRATIVE - the hemisphere with the conical cavity drawn inside it; the stem's 'maximum volume' already fixes the cone. Page idx 6.
rows.solution:
The cone of maximum volume has the hemisphere's flat face as its base and its vertex at the bottom of the hemisphere, so \(r = h = 10\) cm.

Slant height \(l = \sqrt{10^2 + 10^2} = 10\sqrt{2}\) cm.

Curved surface area \(= \pi r l = 3.14 \times 10 \times 10\sqrt{2} = 314\sqrt{2}\ \text{cm}^2\), which is option (A) \(314\sqrt{2}\,\text{cm}^2\).

rows.subtopic: nth Term of an AP
rows.stem: If \(a_n\) represents \(n^{\text{th}}\) term of the A.P. \(-\dfrac{15}{4}, -\dfrac{10}{4}, -\dfrac{5}{4}, \ldots\) then value of \(a_{16} - a_{12}\) is
rows.solution:
The common difference is \(d = -\dfrac{10}{4} - \left(-\dfrac{15}{4}\right) = \dfrac{5}{4}\).

\(a_{16} - a_{12} = (a + 15d) - (a + 11d) = 4d = 4 \times \dfrac{5}{4} = 5\), which is option (C) \(5\).

rows.subtopic: Nature of Roots and the Discriminant
rows.stem: The value of p for which roots of the quadratic equation \(x^2 - px + 6 = 0\) are rational, is
rows.solution:
For \(p = -5\) the equation is \(x^2 + 5x + 6 = 0\), that is \((x + 2)(x + 3) = 0\), with rational roots \(-2\) and \(-3\). Its discriminant \(25 - 24 = 1\) is a perfect square.

The other values fail: \(p = 1\) and \(p = \sqrt{5}\) give a negative discriminant (\(1 - 24\) and \(5 - 24\)), and \(p = 25\) gives \(625 - 24 = 601\), which is not a perfect square.

This is option (B) \(-5\).

rows.subtopic: Sure, Impossible and Complementary Events
rows.stem: Which of the following can not be the probability of an event ?
rows.solution:
A probability always lies between 0 and 1.

\(\dfrac{10}{0.2} = 50 > 1\), so it cannot be a probability. (The others are \(0.39\), \(0.00005\) and \(0.1\).) This is option (C) \(\dfrac{10}{0.2}\).

rows.subtopic: Probability with Cards, Dice and Coins
rows.stem: A card is drawn at random from a well shuffled deck of 52 playing cards. The probability that it is either a ten or a king is
rows.solution:
A deck has 4 tens and 4 kings, so 8 favourable cards.

\(P(\text{a ten or a king}) = \dfrac{8}{52} = \dfrac{2}{13}\), which is option (B) \(\dfrac{2}{13}\).

rows.subtopic: Surface Area of a Combination of Solids
rows.stem: A camping tent in hemispherical shape of radius 1.4 m, has a door opening of area \(0.50\,\text{m}^2\). Outer surface area of the tent is
rows.solution:
The outer surface of the tent is the curved surface of the hemisphere, less the door opening.

\(2\pi r^2 = 2 \times \dfrac{22}{7} \times 1.4 \times 1.4 = 12.32\ \text{m}^2\).

Outer surface area \(= 12.32 - 0.50 = 11.82\ \text{m}^2\), which is option (C) \(11.82\,\text{m}^2\).

rows.subtopic: Area of a Sector
rows.stem: An arc of length 2.2 cm subtends an angle \(\theta\) at the centre of the circle with radius 2.8 cm. The value of \(\theta\) is
rows.solution:
Length of arc \(= \dfrac{\theta}{360^\circ} \times 2\pi r\):

\(2.2 = \dfrac{\theta}{360^\circ} \times 2 \times \dfrac{22}{7} \times 2.8 = \dfrac{\theta}{360^\circ} \times 17.6\), so \(\theta = \dfrac{2.2}{17.6} \times 360^\circ = 45^\circ\).

This is option (C) \(45^\circ\).

rows.subtopic: Trigonometric Ratios of an Acute Angle
rows.stem: For an acute angle \(\theta\), if \(\sin\theta = \dfrac{1}{9}\), then value of \(\dfrac{9\operatorname{cosec}\theta + 1}{9\operatorname{cosec}\theta - 1}\) is
rows.solution:
\(\sin\theta = \dfrac{1}{9}\) gives \(\operatorname{cosec}\theta = 9\), so \(9\operatorname{cosec}\theta = 81\).

\(\dfrac{81 + 1}{81 - 1} = \dfrac{82}{80}\), which is option (D) \(\dfrac{82}{80}\).

rows.subtopic: Criteria for Similarity of Triangles
rows.stem: In the given figure, \(PQ \parallel YZ\) such that XP : PY = 2 : 3. If PQ = 5 cm, then YZ equals
rows.figureNote: REQUIRED - that Q lies on XZ (and P on XY) is shown only in the drawing. Page idx 10.
rows.solution:
\(PQ \parallel YZ\), so \(\Delta XPQ \sim \Delta XYZ\) (AA similarity), and \(\dfrac{PQ}{YZ} = \dfrac{XP}{XY}\).

\(XP : PY = 2 : 3\) gives \(\dfrac{XP}{XY} = \dfrac{2}{5}\). So \(\dfrac{5}{YZ} = \dfrac{2}{5}\) and \(YZ = 12.5\) cm.

This is option (A) \(12.5\) cm.

rows.subtopic: Theoretical Probability and Elementary Events
rows.stem: Meena calculates that the probability of her winning the first prize in a lottery is 0.08. If total 800 tickets were sold, the number of tickets bought by her, is
rows.solution:
If she bought n tickets, \(\dfrac{n}{800} = 0.08\), so \(n = 0.08 \times 800 = 64\).

This is option (A) \(64\).

rows.subtopic: Angle of Elevation Problems
rows.stem: A wire is attached from a point A on the ground to the top of a pole BC, making an angle of elevation as \(60^\circ\). If \(AB = 5\sqrt{3}\) m, then length of the wire is
rows.figureNote: ILLUSTRATIVE - right triangle ABC with the 60 degree angle at A and AB along the ground; every value is in the stem. Page idx 10.
rows.solution:
The wire is AC, the hypotenuse of right triangle ABC, and AB is the side next to the \(60^\circ\) angle.

\(\cos 60^\circ = \dfrac{AB}{AC}\), so \(\dfrac{1}{2} = \dfrac{5\sqrt{3}}{AC}\) and \(AC = 10\sqrt{3}\) m.

This is option (B) \(10\sqrt{3}\) m.

rows.subtopic: Trigonometric Identities
rows.stem: Simplest form of \(\dfrac{\sec A}{\sqrt{\sec^2 A - 1}}\) is
rows.solution:
\(\sec^2 A - 1 = \tan^2 A\), so \(\sqrt{\sec^2 A - 1} = \tan A\) (for an acute angle).

\(\dfrac{\sec A}{\tan A} = \dfrac{1/\cos A}{\sin A/\cos A} = \dfrac{1}{\sin A} = \operatorname{cosec} A\), which is option (C) \(\operatorname{cosec} A\).

rows.chapter: Pair of Linear Equations in Two Variables
rows.subtopic: Consistency from the Ratios of Coefficients
rows.stem:
**Assertion (A) :** The system of linear equations \(3x - 5y + 7 = 0\) and \(-6x + 10y + 14 = 0\) is inconsistent.

**Reason (R) :** When two linear equations don't have unique solution, they always represent parallel lines.
rows.context: Questions number 19 and 20 are Assertion and Reason based questions. Two statements are given, one labelled Assertion (A) and the other labelled Reason (R). Select the correct answer from the codes (A), (B), (C) and (D) as given below :

options.label: A
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: B
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is not the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: C
options.text: Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.

options.label: D
options.text: Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.

rows.solution:
For \(3x - 5y + 7 = 0\) and \(-6x + 10y + 14 = 0\): \(\dfrac{a_1}{a_2} = \dfrac{3}{-6} = -\dfrac{1}{2}\), \(\dfrac{b_1}{b_2} = \dfrac{-5}{10} = -\dfrac{1}{2}\) and \(\dfrac{c_1}{c_2} = \dfrac{7}{14} = \dfrac{1}{2}\).

Since \(\dfrac{a_1}{a_2} = \dfrac{b_1}{b_2} \neq \dfrac{c_1}{c_2}\), the lines are parallel and the system is inconsistent. The Assertion is true.

Two equations without a unique solution may also represent coincident lines (for example \(x + y = 1\) and \(2x + 2y = 2\)), so they are not always parallel. The Reason is false.

The Assertion is true while the Reason is false, which is option (C).

rows.subtopic: HCF and LCM by Prime Factorisation
rows.stem:
**Assertion (A) :** H.C.F. \((36m^2, 18m) = 18m\), where m is a prime number.

**Reason (R) :** H.C.F. of two numbers is always less than or equal to the smaller number.
rows.context: Questions number 19 and 20 are Assertion and Reason based questions. Two statements are given, one labelled Assertion (A) and the other labelled Reason (R). Select the correct answer from the codes (A), (B), (C) and (D) as given below :

options.label: A
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: B
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is not the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: C
options.text: Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.

options.label: D
options.text: Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.

rows.solution:
\(36m^2 = 2^2 \times 3^2 \times m^2\) and \(18m = 2 \times 3^2 \times m\). The common factors, to their lowest powers, give \(2 \times 3^2 \times m = 18m\). The Assertion is true.

The H.C.F. divides each of the two numbers, so it cannot exceed the smaller one. The Reason is true.

But the Reason only bounds the H.C.F.; it is the fact that \(18m\) divides \(36m^2\) that makes the H.C.F. equal to \(18m\). So both statements are true but the Reason does not explain the Assertion, which is option (B).

rows.subtopic: Irrational Numbers and Proof by Contradiction
rows.stem: Prove that \(2 - 5\sqrt{3}\) is an irrational number given that \(\sqrt{3}\) is irrational.
rows.solution:
Suppose, to the contrary, that \(2 - 5\sqrt{3}\) is rational. Then \(2 - 5\sqrt{3} = \dfrac{a}{b}\), where a and b are integers and \(b \neq 0\).

Rearranging, \(\sqrt{3} = \dfrac{2b - a}{5b}\). The right side is a ratio of integers, so it is rational; but \(\sqrt{3}\) is irrational. This is a contradiction.

So the assumption is wrong, and \(2 - 5\sqrt{3}\) is irrational.

rows.subtopic: Distance Formula
rows.stem: Vertices of a right triangle ABC with \(\angle B = 90^\circ\) are \(A(3, 4)\), \(B(1, 1)\) and \(C(-8, 7)\). Find the value of tan A.
rows.solution:
\(BC = \sqrt{(-8 - 1)^2 + (7 - 1)^2} = \sqrt{81 + 36} = \sqrt{117} = 3\sqrt{13}\).

\(AB = \sqrt{(3 - 1)^2 + (4 - 1)^2} = \sqrt{4 + 9} = \sqrt{13}\).

The right angle is at B, so for angle A the opposite side is BC and the adjacent side is AB:

\(\tan A = \dfrac{BC}{AB} = \dfrac{3\sqrt{13}}{\sqrt{13}} = 3\).

rows.subtopic: Distance Formula
rows.stem: Using distance formula, prove that the points \(A(2, 3)\), \(B(-7, 0)\) and \(C(-1, 2)\) are collinear.
rows.solution:
\(AB = \sqrt{(-7 - 2)^2 + (0 - 3)^2} = \sqrt{81 + 9} = \sqrt{90} = 3\sqrt{10}\).

\(BC = \sqrt{(-1 + 7)^2 + (2 - 0)^2} = \sqrt{36 + 4} = \sqrt{40} = 2\sqrt{10}\).

\(AC = \sqrt{(-1 - 2)^2 + (2 - 3)^2} = \sqrt{9 + 1} = \sqrt{10}\).

\(AC + BC = \sqrt{10} + 2\sqrt{10} = 3\sqrt{10} = AB\), so the three points lie on one line: A, B and C are collinear.

rows.subtopic: Criteria for Similarity of Triangles
rows.stem: In the given figure, \(AB \parallel DE\) and \(AC \parallel DF\). Show that \(\Delta ABC \sim \Delta DEF\). If BC = 10 cm, EB = CF = 5 cm and AB = 7 cm, then find the length DE.
rows.figureNote: REQUIRED - that E, B, C and F lie on one line, in that order, is shown only in the drawing. Page idx 14.
rows.solution:
E, B, C and F lie on one line.

\(AB \parallel DE\), so \(\angle DEF = \angle ABC\) (corresponding angles), and \(AC \parallel DF\), so \(\angle DFE = \angle ACB\) (corresponding angles).

So \(\Delta ABC \sim \Delta DEF\) (AA similarity).

\(EF = EB + BC + CF = 5 + 10 + 5 = 20\) cm. Corresponding sides are proportional:

\(\dfrac{BC}{EF} = \dfrac{AB}{DE}\), so \(\dfrac{10}{20} = \dfrac{7}{DE}\) and \(DE = 14\) cm.

rows.subtopic: Trigonometric Ratios of Specific Angles
rows.stem: Evaluate : \(\dfrac{\sin^3 60^\circ - \tan 30^\circ}{\cos^2 45^\circ}\)
rows.solution:
\(\dfrac{\sin^3 60^\circ - \tan 30^\circ}{\cos^2 45^\circ} = \dfrac{\left(\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right)^3 - \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}}}{\left(\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\right)^2} = \dfrac{\dfrac{3\sqrt{3}}{8} - \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{3}}{\dfrac{1}{2}}\)

\(= 2 \times \dfrac{9\sqrt{3} - 8\sqrt{3}}{24} = \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{12}\), which is the same as \(\dfrac{1}{4\sqrt{3}}\).

rows.subtopic: Trigonometric Ratios of Specific Angles
rows.stem: For acute angles A and B and \(A + 2B\) and \(2A + B\) are acute if \(\tan(A + 2B) = \sqrt{3}\) and \(\sin(2A + B) = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\), then find the measures of angles A and B.
rows.solution:
\(\tan(A + 2B) = \sqrt{3}\) with \(A + 2B\) acute gives \(A + 2B = 60^\circ\) ... (1)

\(\sin(2A + B) = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\) with \(2A + B\) acute gives \(2A + B = 45^\circ\) ... (2)

Adding: \(3A + 3B = 105^\circ\), so \(A + B = 35^\circ\). Subtracting (2) from (1): \(B - A = 15^\circ\).

So \(B = 25^\circ\) and \(A = 10^\circ\).

rows.subtopic: Probability from a Collection of Objects
rows.stem: A bag contains 25 balls. Some of them are yellow and others are green. One ball is drawn at random. If probability of getting a green ball is \(3/5\), then find the number of yellow balls.
rows.solution:
\(P(\text{yellow ball}) = 1 - P(\text{green ball}) = 1 - \dfrac{3}{5} = \dfrac{2}{5}\).

So \(\dfrac{\text{number of yellow balls}}{25} = \dfrac{2}{5}\), and the number of yellow balls is \(25 \times \dfrac{2}{5} = 10\).

rows.subtopic: Area of a Sector
rows.stem: A circle of diameter 20 cm is equally divided into five sectors. Find the area and perimeter of one of the sectors.
rows.solution:
The radius is 10 cm. Five equal sectors share \(360^\circ\), so the central angle of each is \(\dfrac{360^\circ}{5} = 72^\circ\).

Area of one sector \(= \dfrac{72}{360} \times \dfrac{22}{7} \times 10 \times 10 = \dfrac{440}{7}\ \text{cm}^2 \approx 62.86\ \text{cm}^2\).

Perimeter of one sector \(=\) arc \(+\) two radii \(= \dfrac{72}{360} \times 2 \times \dfrac{22}{7} \times 10 + 10 + 10 = \dfrac{88}{7} + 20 = \dfrac{228}{7}\) cm \(\approx 32.57\) cm.

rows.subtopic: Sum of First n Terms of an AP
rows.stem: In an A.P., \(15^{\text{th}}\) term exceeds the \(8^{\text{th}}\) term by 21. If sum of first 10 terms is 55, then form the A.P.
rows.solution:
Let the first term be a and the common difference d.

\(a_{15} = a_8 + 21\): \(a + 14d = a + 7d + 21\), so \(7d = 21\) and \(d = 3\).

\(S_{10} = \dfrac{10}{2}[2a + 9 \times 3] = 55\), so \(2a + 27 = 11\) and \(a = -8\).

The A.P. is \(-8, -5, -2, 1, \ldots\)

rows.subtopic: Sum of First n Terms of an AP
rows.stem: The sum of first n terms of an A.P. is \(2n^2 + 13n\). Find its \(n^{\text{th}}\) term and hence \(10^{\text{th}}\) term.

rows.subtopic: Trigonometric Identities
rows.stem: Prove that : \(\dfrac{\tan\theta}{1 - \cot\theta} + \dfrac{\cot\theta}{1 - \tan\theta} = 1 + \tan\theta + \cot\theta\).
rows.solution:
Write everything in sines and cosines:

LHS \(= \dfrac{\sin\theta/\cos\theta}{1 - \cos\theta/\sin\theta} + \dfrac{\cos\theta/\sin\theta}{1 - \sin\theta/\cos\theta} = \dfrac{\sin^2\theta}{\cos\theta(\sin\theta - \cos\theta)} + \dfrac{\cos^2\theta}{\sin\theta(\cos\theta - \sin\theta)}\)

\(= \dfrac{\sin^3\theta - \cos^3\theta}{\sin\theta\cos\theta(\sin\theta - \cos\theta)} = \dfrac{(\sin\theta - \cos\theta)(\sin^2\theta + \cos^2\theta + \sin\theta\cos\theta)}{\sin\theta\cos\theta(\sin\theta - \cos\theta)}\)

\(= \dfrac{\sin^2\theta}{\sin\theta\cos\theta} + \dfrac{\cos^2\theta}{\sin\theta\cos\theta} + \dfrac{\sin\theta\cos\theta}{\sin\theta\cos\theta} = \tan\theta + \cot\theta + 1 =\) RHS.

rows.subtopic: Distance Formula
rows.stem: A circle centered at \((2, 1)\) passes through the points \(A(5, 6)\) and \(B(-3, K)\). Find the value(s) of K. Hence find length of chord AB.

rows.subtopic: Section Formula and Ratio of Division
rows.stem: Prove that the point P dividing the line segment joining the points \(A(-1, 7)\) and \(B(4, -3)\) in the ratio \(3 : 2\), lies on the line \(x - 3y = -1\). Also find length of PA and PB.
rows.solution:
P divides AB with \(AP : PB = 3 : 2\), so by the section formula

\(P = \left(\dfrac{3 \times 4 + 2 \times (-1)}{5}, \dfrac{3 \times (-3) + 2 \times 7}{5}\right) = \left(\dfrac{10}{5}, \dfrac{5}{5}\right) = (2, 1)\).

Substituting \(x = 2\), \(y = 1\) in \(x - 3y\): \(2 - 3(1) = -1\), which is the right side. So P lies on the line \(x - 3y = -1\).

\(PA = \sqrt{(2 + 1)^2 + (1 - 7)^2} = \sqrt{9 + 36} = \sqrt{45} = 3\sqrt{5}\) units.

\(PB = \sqrt{(2 - 4)^2 + (1 + 3)^2} = \sqrt{4 + 16} = \sqrt{20} = 2\sqrt{5}\) units.

rows.chapter: Pair of Linear Equations in Two Variables
rows.subtopic: Graphical Method and Nature of Solutions
rows.stem: Solve the system of linear equations : \(x = 4\) and \(3x - 2y = 6\) graphically.
rows.solution:
\(x = 4\) is the vertical line through \((4, 0)\), parallel to the y-axis.

Points on \(3x - 2y = 6\), that is \(y = \dfrac{3x - 6}{2}\):

| \(x\) | 0 | 2 | 4 |
|---|---|---|---|
| \(y\) | \(-3\) | 0 | 3 |

Plot these points and draw the line through them, and draw the line \(x = 4\) on the same axes. The two lines meet at \((4, 3)\).

The solution is \(x = 4\), \(y = 3\).

rows.subtopic: HCF and LCM by Prime Factorisation
rows.stem: The dimensions of a window are 156 cm \(\times\) 216 cm. Arjun wants to put grill on the window creating complete squares of maximum size. Determine the side length of the square and hence find the number of squares formed.
rows.solution:
The side of the largest square that fits exactly along both edges is the HCF of 156 and 216.

\(156 = 2^2 \times 3 \times 13\) and \(216 = 2^3 \times 3^3\), so HCF \(= 2^2 \times 3 = 12\).

The side of each square is 12 cm.

Number of squares \(= \dfrac{156 \times 216}{12 \times 12} = 13 \times 18 = 234\).

rows.subtopic: Solving a Quadratic Equation by Factorisation
rows.stem: Venkat can row a boat in still water at the speed of 12 km/h. He ferries tourists 15 km upstream and 18 km downstream in 3 hours. Find the speed of the stream.
rows.solution:
Let the speed of the stream be x km/h. The speed upstream is \((12 - x)\) km/h and downstream \((12 + x)\) km/h.

The total time is 3 hours: \(\dfrac{15}{12 - x} + \dfrac{18}{12 + x} = 3\).

\(15(12 + x) + 18(12 - x) = 3(144 - x^2)\), so \(396 - 3x = 432 - 3x^2\), that is \(3x^2 - 3x - 36 = 0\), or \(x^2 - x - 12 = 0\).

\((x - 4)(x + 3) = 0\), so \(x = 4\) or \(x = -3\). A speed cannot be negative, so \(x = 4\).

The speed of the stream is 4 km/h. (Check: \(\dfrac{15}{8} + \dfrac{18}{16} = 1.875 + 1.125 = 3\) hours.)

rows.subtopic: Basic Proportionality Theorem
rows.stem:
D is the mid-point of side BC of \(\Delta ABC\). CE and BF intersect at O, a point on AD. AD is produced to G such that OD = DG. Prove that

(i) OBGC is a parallelogram.

(ii) \(EF \parallel BC\)

(iii) \(\Delta AEF \sim \Delta ABC\)
rows.figureNote: REQUIRED - where E and F lie (E on AB, F on AC, the ends of CE and BF) is shown only in the drawing. Page idx 16.
rows.solution:
(i) D is the mid-point of BC, so \(BD = DC\), and \(OD = DG\) (given). So the diagonals OG and BC of the quadrilateral OBGC bisect each other, and OBGC is a parallelogram.

(ii) Opposite sides of a parallelogram are parallel, so \(CO \parallel GB\). E lies on the line CO, so \(OE \parallel GB\).

In triangle AGB, \(OE \parallel GB\), so by the Basic Proportionality Theorem \(\dfrac{AO}{OG} = \dfrac{AE}{EB}\) ... (1)

Similarly \(BO \parallel GC\), so \(OF \parallel GC\), and in triangle AGC, \(\dfrac{AO}{OG} = \dfrac{AF}{FC}\) ... (2)

From (1) and (2), \(\dfrac{AE}{EB} = \dfrac{AF}{FC}\), so by the converse of the Basic Proportionality Theorem, \(EF \parallel BC\).

(iii) In triangles AEF and ABC: \(\angle AEF = \angle ABC\) (corresponding angles, as \(EF \parallel BC\)), and \(\angle A\) is common.

So \(\Delta AEF \sim \Delta ABC\) (AA similarity).

rows.subtopic: Applications of Similarity
rows.stem:
Through the mid-point Q of side CD of a parallelogram ABCD, the line AR is drawn which intersects BD at P and produced BC at R. Prove that

(i) AQ = QR

(ii) AP = 2PQ

(iii) PR = 2AP
rows.figureNote: ILLUSTRATIVE - parallelogram ABCD with the line AR through Q meeting BD at P and BC produced at R; the stem states the configuration. Page idx 18.
rows.solution:
(i) ABCD is a parallelogram, so \(DC \parallel AB\), that is \(QC \parallel AB\). In triangles RQC and RAB, \(\angle RQC = \angle RAB\) (corresponding angles) and \(\angle R\) is common, so \(\Delta RQC \sim \Delta RAB\).

So \(\dfrac{QR}{AR} = \dfrac{QC}{AB} = \dfrac{1}{2}\), since \(QC = \dfrac{1}{2}CD = \dfrac{1}{2}AB\).

So \(AR = 2QR\), Q is the mid-point of AR, and \(AQ = QR\).

(ii) In triangles PQD and PAB: \(\angle QPD = \angle APB\) (vertically opposite angles) and \(\angle PDQ = \angle PBA\) (alternate angles, as \(DQ \parallel AB\)). So \(\Delta PQD \sim \Delta PAB\).

So \(\dfrac{QP}{AP} = \dfrac{DQ}{BA} = \dfrac{1}{2}\), since \(DQ = \dfrac{1}{2}CD = \dfrac{1}{2}AB\). That is, \(AP = 2PQ\).

(iii) From (i), \(AQ = QR\), so \(AP + PQ = PR - PQ\).

From (ii), \(PQ = \dfrac{1}{2}AP\), so \(AP + \dfrac{1}{2}AP = PR - \dfrac{1}{2}AP\), which gives \(PR = 2AP\).

Number of Tangents from an External Point
rows.stem: PQ and PR are two tangents to a circle with centre O and radius 5 cm. AB is another tangent to the circle at C which lies on OP. If OP = 13 cm, then find the length AB and PA.
rows.figureNote: REQUIRED - that A lies on PQ and B lies on PR is shown only in the drawing. Page idx 18.
rows.solution:
The radius OQ is perpendicular to the tangent PQ, so in right triangle OQP, \(PQ = \sqrt{OP^2 - OQ^2} = \sqrt{169 - 25} = 12\) cm.

C lies on OP and \(OC = 5\) cm, so \(PC = 13 - 5 = 8\) cm.

Let \(AC = x\). Tangents from A are equal, so \(AQ = AC = x\), and \(PA = PQ - AQ = 12 - x\).

AB touches the circle at C, so \(OC \perp AB\), and triangle ACP is right-angled at C:

\(PA^2 = AC^2 + PC^2\), so \((12 - x)^2 = x^2 + 8^2\), that is \(144 - 24x = 64\) and \(x = \dfrac{10}{3}\).

In the same way (tangents from B, with \(PR = 12\) cm), \(BC = \dfrac{10}{3}\) cm.

\(AB = AC + CB = \dfrac{20}{3}\) cm \(\approx 6.67\) cm.

\(PA = 12 - \dfrac{10}{3} = \dfrac{26}{3}\) cm \(\approx 8.67\) cm.

rows.context:

rows.solution:
A is the top of the arch, where it meets the y-axis, so \(x = 0\) there.

rows.subtopic: Geometrical Meaning of the Zeroes of a Polynomial
rows.stem: Find the span of the arch.
rows.context:
An arch of a railway bridge, built on Chenab riverbed, is shown in the above diagram. It is a parabolic arch connecting two hills at P and Q. If the parabolic curve is represented by the polynomial \(p(x) = -0.0025x^2 - 0.025x + 136\).

Observe the diagram and based on above information, answer the following questions :
rows.figureNote: REQUIRED - the coordinates of the arch's end points P and Q are printed only in the drawing. Page idx 20.
rows.solution:
The arch meets the x-axis at \(Q(-238.5, 0)\) and \(P(228.5, 0)\), as shown in the diagram.

Span of the arch \(= 228.5 - (-238.5) = 238.5 + 228.5 = 467\) units.

rows.subtopic: Zeroes and Coefficients of a Quadratic Polynomial
rows.stem: Write the zeroes of the polynomial using diagram and verify the relationship between sum of zeroes and polynomials.
rows.context:
An arch of a railway bridge, built on Chenab riverbed, is shown in the above diagram. It is a parabolic arch connecting two hills at P and Q. If the parabolic curve is represented by the polynomial \(p(x) = -0.0025x^2 - 0.025x + 136\).

Observe the diagram and based on above information, answer the following questions :
rows.figureNote: REQUIRED - the stem asks for the zeroes 'using diagram', and the coordinates of P and Q are printed only in the drawing. Page idx 20.
rows.solution:
The zeroes are the x-coordinates where the arch meets the x-axis. From the diagram they are \(228.5\) and \(-238.5\).

Sum of the zeroes \(= 228.5 + (-238.5) = -10\).

For \(p(x) = -0.0025x^2 - 0.025x + 136\): \(-\dfrac{\text{coefficient of } x}{\text{coefficient of } x^2} = -\dfrac{-0.025}{-0.0025} = -10\).

So the sum of the zeroes equals \(-\dfrac{b}{a}\), as required.

The diagram's coordinates are rounded, so with them the sum checks exactly but the product only approximately (\(228.5 \times (-238.5) = -54497.25\), against \(\dfrac{c}{a} = \dfrac{136}{-0.0025} = -54400\)).

rows.subtopic: Surface Area of a Combination of Solids
rows.stem: Find the surface area of the bulb.
rows.context:
A wall mounted lamp, made of fabric, is shown below. Lamp has cuboidal shape, open from top and bottom. A spherical bulb of diameter 7 cm is latched with a very thin rod. (Ignore the rod while making calculations.)

Dimensions of the cuboid are 24 cm \(\times\) 12 cm \(\times\) 17 cm.
rows.figureNote: ILLUSTRATIVE - the dimensioned drawing of the cuboidal lamp with the bulb inside; every value is in the passage. The photograph beside it is decorative. Page idx 20.
rows.solution:
The bulb has radius \(\dfrac{7}{2}\) cm.

Surface area \(= 4\pi r^2 = 4 \times \dfrac{22}{7} \times \dfrac{7}{2} \times \dfrac{7}{2} = 154\ \text{cm}^2\).

rows.subtopic: Volume of a Combination of Solids
rows.stem: What could be the maximum diameter of the bulb if at least 1 cm space is left from each side ?
rows.context:
A wall mounted lamp, made of fabric, is shown below. Lamp has cuboidal shape, open from top and bottom. A spherical bulb of diameter 7 cm is latched with a very thin rod. (Ignore the rod while making calculations.)

Dimensions of the cuboid are 24 cm \(\times\) 12 cm \(\times\) 17 cm.
rows.solution:
The bulb must fit across the smallest dimension of the lamp, 12 cm, with at least 1 cm left on each side.

Maximum diameter \(= 12 - 2 = 10\) cm.

rows.subtopic: Surface Area of a Combination of Solids
rows.stem: Find the area of the fabric used if there is a fold of 2 cm on top and bottom edges.
rows.context:
A wall mounted lamp, made of fabric, is shown below. Lamp has cuboidal shape, open from top and bottom. A spherical bulb of diameter 7 cm is latched with a very thin rod. (Ignore the rod while making calculations.)

Dimensions of the cuboid are 24 cm \(\times\) 12 cm \(\times\) 17 cm.
rows.solution:
The lamp is open at the top and bottom, so the fabric covers only the four side faces. A fold of 2 cm at the top edge and 2 cm at the bottom edge makes the fabric's height \(17 + 2 + 2 = 21\) cm.

Area of fabric \(= 2 \times 21 \times (24 + 12) = 1512\ \text{cm}^2\).

rows.subtopic: Volume of a Combination of Solids
rows.stem: Find the space available inside the lamp.
rows.context:
A wall mounted lamp, made of fabric, is shown below. Lamp has cuboidal shape, open from top and bottom. A spherical bulb of diameter 7 cm is latched with a very thin rod. (Ignore the rod while making calculations.)

Dimensions of the cuboid are 24 cm \(\times\) 12 cm \(\times\) 17 cm.
rows.solution:
Space available \(=\) volume of the cuboid \(-\) volume of the bulb

\(= 24 \times 12 \times 17 - \dfrac{4}{3} \times \dfrac{22}{7} \times \dfrac{7}{2} \times \dfrac{7}{2} \times \dfrac{7}{2} = 4896 - \dfrac{539}{3}\)

\(= \dfrac{14149}{3}\ \text{cm}^3 \approx 4716.33\ \text{cm}^3\).

rows.subtopic: Angle of Depression Problems
rows.stem: Write a relation between d (the height of window) and y.
rows.context:
Elevated water storage tanks are built to store and supply water to nearby colonies. In the diagram given above, AB is an elevated water tank and CD is a nearby multistorey building. The building is 54 metres away from the water tank.

From a window (W) of the building, the angle of elevation of top of the tank is \(45^\circ\) and angle of depression of its foot is \(30^\circ\).
rows.figureNote: REQUIRED - the labels h, d, x and y and the point X are defined only in the drawing. The photograph beside it is decorative. Page idx 22.
rows.solution:
In the diagram, X is the point on the tank AB level with the window W, so \(XW\) is horizontal, \(XA = d\) and \(WA = y\).

The angle of depression of the foot A from W is \(30^\circ\), so \(\angle XWA = 30^\circ\). In right triangle WXA:

\(\sin 30^\circ = \dfrac{XA}{WA}\), so \(\dfrac{1}{2} = \dfrac{d}{y}\), that is \(y = 2d\).

rows.subtopic: Angle of Elevation Problems
rows.stem: Determine the value of h.
rows.context:
Elevated water storage tanks are built to store and supply water to nearby colonies. In the diagram given above, AB is an elevated water tank and CD is a nearby multistorey building. The building is 54 metres away from the water tank.

From a window (W) of the building, the angle of elevation of top of the tank is \(45^\circ\) and angle of depression of its foot is \(30^\circ\).
rows.figureNote: REQUIRED - the labels h, d, x and y and the point X are defined only in the drawing. The photograph beside it is decorative. Page idx 22.
rows.solution:
XW is horizontal and equal to the distance between the tank and the building, so \(XW = AC = 54\) m. In the diagram \(BX = h\), and the angle of elevation of the top B from W is \(45^\circ\).

In right triangle BXW: \(\tan 45^\circ = \dfrac{BX}{XW}\), so \(1 = \dfrac{h}{54}\) and \(h = 54\) m.

rows.subtopic: Angle of Elevation Problems
rows.stem: Determine height of the water tank.
rows.context:
Elevated water storage tanks are built to store and supply water to nearby colonies. In the diagram given above, AB is an elevated water tank and CD is a nearby multistorey building. The building is 54 metres away from the water tank.

From a window (W) of the building, the angle of elevation of top of the tank is \(45^\circ\) and angle of depression of its foot is \(30^\circ\).
rows.figureNote: REQUIRED - the labels h, d, x and y and the point X are defined only in the drawing. The photograph beside it is decorative. Page idx 22.
rows.solution:
XW is horizontal, with \(XW = AC = 54\) m, and the angle of elevation of the top B from W is \(45^\circ\). In right triangle BXW: \(\tan 45^\circ = \dfrac{h}{54}\), so \(h = BX = 54\) m.

The angle of depression of the foot A from W is \(30^\circ\). In right triangle WXA: \(\tan 30^\circ = \dfrac{d}{54}\), so \(\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}} = \dfrac{d}{54}\) and \(d = XA = \dfrac{54}{\sqrt{3}} = 18\sqrt{3}\) m.

Height of the tank \(= h + d = (54 + 18\sqrt{3})\) m.

rows.subtopic: Angle of Elevation Problems
rows.stem: Find the value of \(x\) and height of the window above ground level.
rows.context:
Elevated water storage tanks are built to store and supply water to nearby colonies. In the diagram given above, AB is an elevated water tank and CD is a nearby multistorey building. The building is 54 metres away from the water tank.

From a window (W) of the building, the angle of elevation of top of the tank is \(45^\circ\) and angle of depression of its foot is \(30^\circ\).
rows.figureNote: REQUIRED - the labels h, d, x and y and the point X are defined only in the drawing. The photograph beside it is decorative. Page idx 22.
rows.solution:
The angle of depression of the foot A from W equals the angle of elevation of W from A, so \(\angle WAC = 30^\circ\). In right triangle WCA, with \(AC = 54\) m:

\(\tan 30^\circ = \dfrac{WC}{AC}\), so \(\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}} = \dfrac{WC}{54}\) and \(WC = 18\sqrt{3}\) m. The window is \(18\sqrt{3}\) m above the ground.

In right triangle BXW, \(XW = 54\) m and \(\angle BWX = 45^\circ\), so \(BX = h = 54\) m (as \(\tan 45^\circ = 1\)), and \(x = WB\) is the hypotenuse:

\(\sin 45^\circ = \dfrac{h}{x}\), so \(\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} = \dfrac{54}{x}\) and \(x = 54\sqrt{2}\) m.
